definition.en: Everything Semina Verbi covers: the expressions of human culture, from the arts to the sciences, and the Gospel themes they carry.
Themes of the Gospel and of Christian life that a work explores, grouped after the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
Creative practices and their works, following UNESCO's cultural domains: literature, the performing, visual and audiovisual arts, architecture, crafts, cultural heritage and gastronomy.
Written and oral works of imagination and of artful prose, in any language. Studies about literature belong under Literary studies.
Works in verse: lyric, epic, dramatic and sacred poetry, hymns and song lyrics read as poems.
Book-length works of narrative prose fiction.
Short narrative prose fiction: short stories, novellas, tales and fables.
Plays and other dramatic works as written texts. Their staging belongs under Theatre.
Non-fiction prose of literary value: essays, letters, memoirs, autobiographies, spiritual writings published as literature.
Literature written for children and young readers, in any form.
Arts performed live before an audience: music, theatre, dance and their combined forms.
Musical works, songs, albums and performers. Studies about music belong under Musicology.
Art music of the Western tradition and its concert repertoire: symphonies, chamber music, concertos, art songs.
Music for worship or on religious texts: chant, masses, oratorios, hymns, gospel and contemporary Christian music.
Commercial music of mass audiences: pop, rock, folk-rock, country, singer-songwriters, soundtracks released as songs.
Traditional music transmitted within a people or region.
The staging and performance of plays and theatrical shows. Plays as texts belong under Drama.
Dance works and forms: ballet, modern dance, folk and liturgical dance.
Stage musicals combining songs, spoken dialogue and dance.
Staged works sung throughout with orchestra: opera, operetta, and their libretti as staged works.
Arts that produce works to be seen: painting, sculpture, drawing, printmaking, photography.
Works of paint applied to a surface, by technique.
Painting on fresh plaster, including church and palace cycles.
Painting with oil-based paints, on canvas or panel.
Painting with water-soluble pigments on paper.
Painted sacred images of the Eastern and Western Christian traditions, especially icons on panel.
Prehistoric painting and engraving on rock surfaces.
Three-dimensional works carved, modelled or cast, in any material.
Works made by drawing on a surface with dry or wet media.
Drawings made with charcoal.
Drawings made with graphite or coloured pencils.
Works printed from a matrix: engraving, etching, woodcut, lithography.
Prints from lines cut into a plate or block.
Prints from lines bitten into a metal plate by acid.
Photographic works and photographers, by genre or technique.
Photographs in monochrome.
Photographs made with high-dynamic-range technique.
Photographs whose subject is natural or built landscape.
Photographs whose subject is a person or group.
Sequential art telling a story in drawn panels: comic strips, comic books, graphic novels, manga.
Applied and decorative arts producing crafted objects: ceramics, glass, mosaic, textiles, metalwork, calligraphy.
Pottery, porcelain and other fired-clay works.
Works made of or in glass.
Objects formed by blowing molten glass.
Coloured glass windows and panels, in churches and elsewhere.
Images made of small pieces of stone, glass or ceramic set in a surface.
Woven textile images and other textile arts such as embroidery.
Works in gold, silver and precious metals, including liturgical vessels and reliquaries.
Artistic lettering and the decoration of manuscripts.
Buildings and the art of designing them, by type and style. The engineering of structures belongs under Civil engineering.
Churches, cathedrals, monasteries, shrines and other places of worship.
Gardens, parks and designed landscapes.
The design of objects and visual communication.
Visual communication by typography, images and layout.
The design of mass-produced objects.
Works made to be watched, heard or played on a screen or broadcast: film, television, radio, animation, video games.
Motion pictures released as films, and filmmakers. Genres are not categories; they go in the infobox.
Fiction films of full length.
Films of short length.
Non-fiction films.
Television series, miniseries, sitcoms and programmes. Genres are not categories.
Radio programmes and dramas.
Animated films and series, by any technique.
Interactive games played on a screen, and their makers.
Inherited tangible and intangible culture: monuments, traditions, festivals, folklore and symbols of peoples.
Historic buildings, sites and memorials as heritage.
Customs, rites and practices handed down within a culture.
Recurring celebrations, popular feasts and festivals.
Myths, legends, fairy tales and popular beliefs of peoples.
How Christianity shaped the culture, institutions and identity of Europe.
Flags, coats of arms and other symbols of peoples, states and institutions.
Food, cooking, wine and the culture of the table.
The study of human culture and thought, following OECD Fields of Science group 6: history, languages and literature, philosophy, theology, the study of the arts.
The study of the human past and historical works, by period.
From the beginnings of writing to the end of Antiquity.
The Middle Ages, about 500 to 1500.
About 1500 to the end of the eighteenth century.
From the end of the eighteenth century to the present.
The history of the Church and of Christianity.
The study of the human past through material remains.
The scientific study of language and of particular languages.
Literary theory, criticism and the history of literature. Literary works themselves belong under Literature.
Philosophical works, thinkers and disciplines.
Being, causes, God as known by reason, the nature of reality.
Knowledge, truth and certainty.
Philosophical moral reflection: the good, virtue, duty, natural law.
Ethical questions of life, medicine and biotechnology.
The study of valid reasoning and argument.
Beauty, art and taste as philosophical questions.
The common good, justice, authority and the state as philosophical questions.
The study of God and of revelation in the light of faith, as an academic discipline. Religious life and practice belong under Religion.
Exegesis, interpretation and the history of the books of the Bible.
The doctrines of faith: Trinity, Christ, Church, sacraments, last things.
Christian moral life in the light of faith, including Catholic social teaching.
The Fathers of the Church and their writings.
Prayer, mysticism and the spiritual life.
The study of the visual arts and architecture through history.
The study of music, its history and theory.
The study and criticism of film and other audiovisual media.
The study of human behaviour and society, following OECD Fields of Science group 5.
The study of the mind and behaviour.
The study of production, exchange and use of goods, and of business.
Teaching, schooling and formation.
Society, social groups, family and social change.
Cultural and social anthropology: the comparative study of peoples and cultures.
Legal systems, laws and jurisprudence, including canon law.
Government, politics, international relations and public policy.
The study of places, peoples and their environments.

names.fr: Sciences de l'information et de la communication

definition.en: Journalism, mass media and social communication.
The sciences of nature and of formal systems, following OECD Fields of Science group 1: mathematics, computer science, physics, astronomy, chemistry, earth and life sciences.
Number, quantity, structure, space and change.
Computation, algorithms, software and information.
Matter, energy, forces and their laws.
Celestial bodies and the universe, including cosmology.
The composition, structure and reactions of substances.
The planet Earth and its environment.
Rocks, minerals and the history of the Earth.
Weather and climate.
The natural environment and human impact on it.
Living organisms and life processes.
Plants.
Animals.
Genes, heredity and variation.
Relations of organisms with each other and their environment.
The design and making of structures, machines, systems and materials, following OECD Fields of Science group 2.
Structures, construction, transport infrastructure.
Machines, engines and mechanical systems.
Electricity, electronics and telecommunications.
Computers, networks, the internet and software as technology in use.
Aircraft and spacecraft.
Technology using living organisms, including genetic engineering.

names.es: Ciencias médicas y de la salud
names.fr: Sciences médicales et de la santé

definition.en: Human health and its care, following OECD Fields of Science group 3.
The diagnosis, treatment and prevention of disease.
The care of the sick.
The health of populations: epidemics, prevention, health systems.
Drugs and their effects.
Religious traditions and their life, worship, persons and art as expressions of culture. Theology as an academic discipline belongs under Humanities.
The Christian faith as lived: churches, worship, saints, religious life.
The public worship of the Church: Mass, sacraments, the liturgical year, the Liturgy of the Hours.
Saints, blesseds and venerable servants of God, and their lives.
Monastic orders, congregations and other forms of consecrated life.
Art made for worship and devotion, considered as religious expression.
The Popes and the papacy.
Orthodox, Protestant and other Christian churches and communities.
The books of Sacred Scripture, their persons and stories as such.
The Jewish religion and its traditions.
The Islamic religion and its traditions.
Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism, Shinto and other religions of Asia.
Indigenous and ancient religions, including the religions of Greece and Rome.
Recent religious movements, esotericism and New Age.
Everyday mass culture that is not itself an art form: sport, fashion, games and toys, fandom, internet culture.
Sports, athletes and competitions.
Clothing, style and the fashion industry.
Toys, board and card games and other non-digital games.
Fan communities and their creative practices.
Memes, online communities, influencers and social media phenomena.
The virtues given by God that unite us to him: faith, hope and charity (CCC 1812–1829).
Believing God and all he has revealed; trust and fidelity in him, doubt and the search for faith.
Desiring eternal life and trusting in God's promises against despair.
Love of God above all and of neighbour as oneself; self-giving love, love of enemies.
The human virtues on which moral life hinges: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance (CCC 1805–1809).
Practical wisdom: discerning the true good and the right means.
Giving God and neighbour their due; fairness, rights, the struggle against injustice.
Courage and constancy in doing good, facing fear, trial and persecution.
Mastery of desires and appetites; chastity, sobriety, self-control.
The drama of sin and of God's saving grace: fall, temptation, conversion, forgiveness, redemption.
Evil chosen against God and neighbour, its roots and consequences.
Enticement to evil and the struggle to resist it.
Sorrow for sin and the resolve to amend one's life.
Turning one's whole life back to God; a change of heart.
Pardoning others and being pardoned; reconciliation after offence.
Compassion that goes beyond justice, God's and ours; works of mercy.
Being bought back from sin and death; a life redeemed.
God's free and undeserved gift that heals and sanctifies.
Giving one's life or goods for others or for God; self-sacrificial love.
The dignity and destiny of the human being created in God's image (CCC 1700–1876).
The inner voice judging good and evil; its formation and fidelity to it.
Free will, responsibility and true freedom for the good.
The worth of every person from conception to natural death.
Pain, illness, loss and the meaning of suffering.
Mortality, dying and facing death.
The last things: judgment, heaven, hell, purgatory, the resurrection of the body.
God's call to each person and its discernment.
Life with others: family, marriage, friendship, community, work, peace and creation.
Parents and children, family bonds and their trials.
The covenant of man and woman, fidelity and conjugal love.
Bonds of friendship, loyalty and companionship.
Belonging, solidarity and the common good of a group or people.
Human labour, its dignity and its meaning.
Peace and war, violence and nonviolence, reconciliation between peoples.
Nature as God's gift and the human responsibility for it.
The mysteries of Christ and the life of the Church as they appear in a work.
God made man; Christmas and the hidden life of Jesus.
The Passion and death of Christ; carrying one's cross.
The Resurrection of Christ and new life over death.
The Mass, Holy Communion and Eucharistic devotion.
The Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and Marian devotion.
The call to be holy; the witness of saints and martyrs.
Speaking with God; prayer, contemplation and worship.
